source_read: PMC HTML (PMC5032490; World Psychiatry 2016;15(3):195-204), the published version (courtesy of the World Psychiatric Association; no author-manuscript banner), read in my own browser tab on 2026-10-31 (title checked); full page text saved to my folder and read start to end: abstract, untitled introduction, sections on cannabinoids and the endocannabinoid system, the changing nature of recreational cannabinoids, psychosis (with Table 1, rendered as text), criticisms of the causal hypothesis, genetic predisposition, mechanism, outcome and treatment, other psychiatric disorders, brain and cognition, adolescents, therapeutic use, conclusions, and the reference list (166 entries). The article has no figures. No funding or conflict-of-interest statement appears in the saved page text. A narrative review: everything it reports from other studies is second-hand.

claims.overstatement: None. If anything the claim understates Murray's position slightly: Murray calls cannabis a component (contributory) cause and says the evidence is sufficient for public-health messages about the risk, especially of regular high-potency and synthetic-cannabinoid use; 'strong enough for a public-health message that cannabis can increase the risk' is Gage et al.'s phrase, which Murray quotes and adopts. The claim's grouping is fair as a description of how this review reads the evidence.
claims.note: Murray is from the same group as several studies it relies on (the south London case-control studies; its last author is Di Forti), and it rebuts the sceptical readings (Ksir & Hart, 2016; Hill, 2015; Haney & Evins, 2016) without new data. It reports no Mendelian randomization or co-relative study. Its genetic discussion describes schizophrenia polygenic risk as explaining only a very small share of cannabis use (Power et al., 2014, second-hand), which is in the same direction as the claim's 'genetic liability to schizophrenia making cannabis use more likely', but Murray treats it as minor. The Andreasson et al. (1987) figure, six times the risk with more than 50 occasions over 15 years in 45,750 conscripts, is given without saying whether it is adjusted; from general knowledge, not from this source, six is the unadjusted relative risk, which fell to about 2.3 after adjustment in the original paper, an example of the attenuation the claim describes (to be checked at the original if used). Table 1's adjusted odds ratios for 13 longitudinal analyses range from 1.1 (0.76-1.65) to 4.5 (1.1-18.2); the Henquet entry is printed 1.7 (1.1-1.5), an interval that excludes its own estimate.

anchors.extracted: The review states that epidemiology shows an association and a dose-response with later psychosis; that high-potency cannabis and synthetic cannabinoids carry the greatest risk; that argument continues over how genetic predisposition is correlated with or interacts with use and over the preventable share; and that the evidence for cannabis as a component cause is now sufficient for public-health messages about risk.

anchors.locator: Criticisms of the causal hypothesis, 1st to 4th paragraphs
anchors.extracted: Most European and Australasian experts are said to be convinced cannabis is one of several contributory causes of schizophrenia; three sceptical North American articles are named (refs 80-82). Rebuttals without figures: the Dunedin cohort adjusted for psychotic symptoms at age 11; in Christchurch people smoked less once minor symptoms developed; patients report the same hedonic reasons for use; other drug use and tobacco did not remove the association (refs 58, 66, 67).

anchors.locator: Genetic predisposition or gene x environment interaction?, 1st to 3rd paragraphs
anchors.extracted: Shared genetic vulnerability is called a popular explanation; psychotic relatives of cannabis-using patients often also use cannabis; the schizophrenia polygenic score explained only a very small share of cannabis use in an Australian sample (Power et al.); no study had yet tested a polygenic score by cannabis interaction; patients carrying large rare deletions less often had comorbid cannabis abuse, read as support for a threshold model. No effect sizes given.

No animal model can prove an environmental cause; the authors ask whether waiting for absolute proof is sensible; they quote Gage et al.'s conclusion that epidemiological evidence warrants a public-health message that cannabis can increase the risk of psychotic disorders; they add that knowledge should not be overstated, that it is uncertain how far cannabis induces psychosis without genetic vulnerability, and that estimates of the preventable share range from 8% to 24% (citing only ref 66).

Andreasson et al.: 45,750 Swedish conscripts; more than 50 occasions of use carried six times the risk of schizophrenia over 15 years, adjustment not stated. Nine of twelve longitudinal studies found a significant association with psychotic symptoms or illness and three a non-significant trend; Table 1 lists adjusted ORs of 1.1 (0.76-1.65) to 4.5 (1.1-18.2), the Henquet row misprinted as 1.7 (1.1-1.5).

claims.overstatement: Slight, for the polygenic-score sentence. The review says only that Di Forti et al. examined schizophrenia polygenic scores in people using low- and high-potency cannabis and found no evidence that high-potency users were more genetically predisposed; it gives no sample size or figures, and its reference 90 is the authors' reply in Lancet Psychiatry correspondence (2015;2:382), not a peer-reviewed report. 'Did not differ' asserts a null result that the review does not show; suggested wording: 'reported finding no evidence that schizophrenia polygenic scores were higher in people using high-potency cannabis (from the team's own correspondence reply; no figures given)'.
claims.note: Murray's description of the 2015 south London study gives 410 first-episode patients and 390 healthy controls, while the claim gives 370 controls, so the control count should be checked at Di Forti et al. (2015) itself, which I could not read (check page at the publisher). Murray summarizes that study as daily high-potency use carrying five times the odds and hashish use no increased risk, and suggests the latter may reflect hashish's lower THC and its cannabidiol, a speculation, since cannabidiol was not measured. In its Conclusions, Murray gives the share of psychosis that could be prevented if nobody used cannabis as 8% to 24%, citing only the 2015 study; per Di Forti et al. (2019, Research in context panel) the 24% is that study's figure for high-potency use, so Murray's framing mislabels it as a fraction for all cannabis use, and states no causal assumption. THC figures in the review (rise from 3% or less in the 1960s; about 16% in England and 20% in the Netherlands in the early 2000s; high-THC plants with only traces of cannabidiol) are second-hand.

anchors.locator: Genetic predisposition or gene x environment interaction?, 2nd paragraph; references 89 and 90
anchors.extracted: Gage et al. (correspondence, Lancet Psychiatry 2015;2:380) suggested people using high-potency cannabis might be especially genetically predisposed; Di Forti et al. (authors' reply, Lancet Psychiatry 2015;2:382) examined the schizophrenia polygenic score in users of low- and high-potency cannabis and found no evidence for this. No n or effect size given.

The 2015 south London study is described as 410 patients with first-episode psychotic disorder and 390 healthy controls; daily high-potency use carried five times the odds of psychotic disorder compared with no use; hashish use was not associated, possibly (the authors suggest) because of lower THC and the presence of cannabidiol.
Estimates of the share of psychosis that could be prevented if nobody used cannabis are given as 8% to 24%, citing only ref 66 (Di Forti et al., 2015); no causal assumption is stated.

anchors.locator: The changing nature of recreational cannabinoids, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
anchors.extracted: Second-hand: THC in herbal cannabis and resin was 3% or less in the 1960s; sinsemilla ('skunk') bred for THC carries only traces of cannabidiol; mean THC about 16% in England and 20% in the Netherlands in the early 2000s, about 15% in Australia, 12% in the US by 2014.

claims.overstatement: None for the part Murray supports. Attribution precision: the claim cites Murray together with Hall & Degenhardt (2009) and Hall (2015) after a list of five studies, but Murray describes only the south-east London study (and the sceptics' argument in general terms); the Australian and English modelling studies, Zurich and the general-practice study are not in Murray.
claims.note: Murray supports the south-east London part: incidence of schizophrenia described as doubling between 1965 and 1999, with the share of patients with schizophrenia who used cannabis rising more than among other psychiatric patients (Boydell et al., 2006, ref 85; the location comes from the reference title). Murray calls it the only competent study spanning several decades with constant research criteria, and uses it against the sceptical argument that incidence did not change while use rose; it also says reliable information on trends in incidence is scarce, which supports 'evidence is insufficient'. Murray does not mention the ecological nature of the comparison. No numbers beyond 'doubled' and the dates.

anchors.locator: Criticisms of the causal hypothesis, 5th paragraph; reference 85
anchors.extracted: The sceptics' argument that use rose in the late 20th century without a change in schizophrenia incidence is answered: there is little reliable information on incidence trends; the only study spanning decades with the same research criteria (Boydell et al., 2006, south-east London) found incidence doubled from 1965 to 1999 and the proportion of patients with schizophrenia using cannabis rose disproportionately compared with other psychiatric patients.

risk_of_bias.note: Editors' narrative-review checklist, overall high: no search or selection criteria, no appraisal, heavy reliance on the authors' own studies (13 of 166 references by my count too), and an unbalanced treatment of shared-liability and reverse-causation evidence.

interpretation_gap.note: 'Substantial' fits and the quoted abstract phrase is exact. One wording correction: the card's '(8-24%, from the authors' own study, assuming causality)' may read as though Murray states the causal assumption; Murray states none, and presents the range as the share preventable if nobody used cannabis.

missed: The 24% in the 8-24% range is, per Di Forti et al. (2019, Research in context panel), the 2015 study's attributable fraction for high-potency cannabis, while Murray presents the range as the share of psychosis preventable if nobody used cannabis (Conclusions, 3rd paragraph), with no causal assumption stated. Murray mislabels the exposure, beyond the selection of the range that reporting issue 6 notes.

Andreasson et al. (1987): Murray's 'six times' (Psychosis, 2nd paragraph) is given without its adjustment status; from general knowledge, not from this source, it is the unadjusted relative risk for more than 50 occasions, about 2.3 after adjustment in the original paper. To be checked at the primary before any claim uses it.

Murray presents the polygenic finding on potency from its own correspondence reply (ref 90) without figures and as 'no evidence to support' the predisposition hypothesis; the card's replication timeline turns this into 'finding no difference in polygenic scores', which is stronger than the review's wording.
